strengths: Significance: Learning when a solver has already found a sufficiently good incumbent addresses a useful bottleneck in repeated mixed-integer optimization. The method can use inexpensive solver statistics without requiring the full problem formulation.

Originality: Calibrating an early-stopping rule over entire solver trajectories is a promising application of conformal prediction, distinct from calibrating the outputs of an independent learned heuristic.

Empirical merits: Experiments cover six problem families and two commercial solvers. Appendix A reports substantial Gurobi runtime reductions, including 431.8 to 96.2 seconds on OTS and 221.0 to 11.7 seconds on MIS, with respective test success rates of 96.4% and 97%.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and training/calibration/deployment pipeline are understandable. The limitations appropriately acknowledge expensive training-data generation, dependence on the instance distribution, and variation in speedup across families. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect conformal rank bound: Lemma 4.2 claims P[Z_new ≥ Z_[c+1−n]] ≥ (n+1)/(c+1), whereas for continuous iid variables the probability is n/(c+1). For c=n=1, the claimed bound is 1 although the probability is 1/2. The subsequent calibration instruction uses the incorrect stronger bound. With c=100 it permits n=95, yielding only 95/101 ≈ 94.06% under the corrected rank calculation, rather than 95%.

Soundness—Theorem 4.1 itself fails at threshold boundaries: Equation (2) is not a valid equivalence for general nonincreasing functions, and the supremum of safe thresholds need not be safe. For example, let every instance have true gap and prediction equal to 1 before time 1 and 0 afterward, with epsilon between 0 and 1. Every threshold k<1 stops safely at time 1, but their supremum kappa=1 stops at time 0 and fails on every instance. This satisfies the stated convergence assumptions and contradicts the theorem. Correct treatment of discontinuities, ties, and strict versus non-strict stopping inequalities is essential to the central guarantee.

Soundness—additional guarantees are not established by the supplied arguments: Theorem 5.1 applies a fixed-u VC bound and then takes a supremum over all u without establishing a simultaneous event; its proof also contains a sqrt(2) factor absent from the statement. Theorem 5.2 assumes empirical success at least 1−alpha, which does not follow from the manuscript's rule for choosing n. These results require revised proofs after correcting the calibration construction.

Evaluation does not convincingly establish the advertised reliability. Appendix A reports only 88% success for CP GRB on MVC and 85%, 78.6%, 80%, and 91% for CP COPT on GISP, OTS, MMCN, and MIS. A single split below 95% does not itself disprove marginal coverage, but these outcomes require repeated calibration splits and uncertainty estimates. Figure 4 instead evaluates the looser 0.2% tolerance, while the principal claim concerns 0.1%.

Practical significance is incompletely tested. Presolve is disabled throughout, so the reported speedups do not establish gains over normally configured solvers. Stopping after one or three incumbents provides weak quality-matched baselines. Comparisons with calibrated time limits, incumbent-stagnation rules, and relaxed solver-gap thresholds would clarify the value of the learned predictor. Callback inference overhead and the cost of generating training labels also need clearer accounting.

Reproducibility and mathematical presentation need substantial repair. Section 4 trains an absolute-gap predictor with a squashing function, whereas Section 6 describes a direct network output and the theoretical target is a relative gap. Section 5 defines suboptimality by subtracting the optimal objective from an already defined gap. The inverse-gap weighting is undefined when the incumbent is optimal, with no stabilization specified. The promised code link is absent, important training settings are missing, and the treatment of true optimal labels for time-limited solves is unclear. These ambiguities prevent reliable reconstruction of the evaluated method.

For identical trajectories with true gap 1 before time 1 and 0 afterward, and prediction 0.5 before time 1 and 0 afterward, every threshold below 0.5 stops safely, but their supremum 0.5 stops immediately and fails. Thus the theorem can have zero success probability under its stated assumptions. Equation (2) incorrectly handles equality and plateaus; these are especially relevant to callback-based solver trajectories. A corrected stopping rule and proof are essential.

Theorem 5.2 assumes that the selected supremum attains the required empirical success rate, which the preceding construction does not ensure. One split below 95% does not by itself disprove a marginal conformal guarantee, but these results require discussion and repeated calibration/test splits with uncertainty estimates. Figure 4 instead evaluates 0.2% tolerance, despite the central 0.1% claim; success at that relaxed tolerance does not validate the advertised target.

Evaluation and significance: Presolve is disabled for both solvers, so the speedups do not establish improvements over typical solver configurations. The early-stopping baselines return after one or three solutions and have essentially zero target accuracy. Comparisons with calibrated time limits, incumbent-stagnation rules, relaxed solver gaps, and simpler predictors are needed to determine the benefit of the learned trajectory model at comparable solution quality.

Reproducibility: The promised code link in Section 6.1 is absent. Learning rate, batch size, training duration in epochs, random seeds, feature normalization, and callback sampling details are insufficiently specified. The inverse-gap loss weight is undefined when the training gap is zero, with no regularization described. It is also unclear how certified optimal labels are obtained for instances reaching the 600-second limit and how inference overhead is measured.

Presentation and implementation consistency: The manuscript alternates between relative gap, absolute objective gap, and a predictor denoted by the same symbol as the true gap. Section 5 defines suboptimality by subtracting the optimal objective from an already defined gap. Section 4.2 uses a bounded squashing function, whereas Section 6 describes the predictor directly as the network output. These discrepancies obscure which algorithm was implemented and whether the theoretical assumptions apply. The loss uses weights proportional to 1/y despite y becoming zero after an optimal incumbent is found. The theoretical squashed predictor differs from the directly parameterized predictor in the experiments, and the manuscript does not explain how exact training/test optima are obtained for time-limited solves or how inference overhead is included.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Relative and absolute gaps are interchanged across Sections 3–5; OTS is inconsistently named; and the MVC results are duplicated under 'Maximum vertex capacity.' These ambiguities make it difficult to reconstruct precisely what was implemented. Overall, the useful idea and promising speedups do not compensate for unresolved errors in the central guarantee.

strengths: Significance: Learning when to stop a solver addresses a useful practical problem: finding a near-optimal incumbent can be much faster than certifying it. The reported Gurobi runtime reductions are substantial, including 221.0 to 11.7 seconds on MIS and 245.2 to 83.9 seconds on MMCN.

Originality: Calibrating a stopping rule over entire solver trajectories is a worthwhile application of conformal prediction. The distinction from pointwise prediction and independent learned heuristics is meaningful, even though the underlying calibration tools are established.

Evaluation: The experiments cover six problem families and two commercial solvers. Appendix C includes useful comparisons with linear predictors, incumbent-improvement heuristics, and relaxed solver tolerances; Appendix D investigates calibration size and distribution perturbations.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and pipeline are understandable. The manuscript candidly acknowledges training-data costs, dependence on the instance distribution, and variation in speedups. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 4.1 is false as stated, undermining the central guarantee. Consider identical instances whose true gap and predicted gap both equal 1 for t < 1 and 0 thereafter, with epsilon < 1. Every threshold k in [0,1) stops safely at t = 1, so the theorem selects their supremum, kappa = 1. However, the stated stopping rule uses predicted gap <= kappa and therefore stops at t = 0, failing with probability one. The proof incorrectly treats a supremum as an attained safe maximum, and equivalence (2) fails at plateaus and jumps. These are directly relevant to callback-based solver trajectories. The calibration score, threshold convention, and proof need a consistent correction.

Soundness—Theorem 5.1 also has an unresolved proof gap. A VC bound uniform over kappa for each fixed u does not automatically hold simultaneously over the supremum across u taken in the proof. A valid argument for the relevant function class is needed. Theorem 5.3 additionally claims an additive rho correction for Theorem 5.1, whereas bounded expected suboptimality and runtime generally require corrections scaled by Smax and Tmax, respectively.

Evidence for coverage is insufficiently reconciled with the claims. Appendix B reports only 88% correctness for CP GRB on MVC, and 85%, 78.6%, 80%, and 91% for CP COPT on GISP, OTS, MMCN, and MIS. A single split below 95% does not itself refute marginal conformal validity, but these outcomes require explicit discussion and repeated-calibration evaluation for the reported configurations. Figure 4 measures 0.2%-optimality rather than the claimed 0.1% target. Appendix D helps, but uses different generated settings and includes c = 5 and 10, for which no n <= c can satisfy the prescribed n/(c+1) >= 0.95; the fallback procedure is unspecified.

Experimental validity: Presolve is disabled for both solvers, and Gurobi is configured with MIPFocus = 1, favoring incumbent discovery. This may enlarge precisely the discovery-versus-certification gap the method exploits. Comparisons are useful within that configuration, but default-presolve and representative solver settings are needed to establish practical reach. The manuscript should also clarify whether reported wall-clock times include all predictor and callback overhead.

Reproducibility: The code-availability sentence ends without a link. Important implementation details are missing, including learning rate, batch size, feature normalization, callback sequence handling, and numerical threshold selection. Equation (5) assigns weight proportional to 1/y despite y becoming exactly zero after the optimum is found; its implemented regularization is essential. Section 4.2 also switches from relative gap to an absolute-gap training target without clearly distinguishing the quantities.

Data and ground-truth provenance are unclear. Table 1 lists 800 OTS training instances while its caption says only 100 instances are available in total. The OTS correctness percentages also appear consistent with a denominator of 28 rather than the stated 72 test instances. Because solves are capped at 600 seconds and may return an incumbent, the paper must explain how true optimal values were obtained for training, calibration, and evaluation, and how unresolved instances were handled.

Overall, the application and runtime results are promising, but the manuscript's defining contribution is a rigorous solution-quality guarantee. The invalid central theorem, incomplete implementation specification, and unresolved coverage evidence prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Significance: Learning when an incumbent is sufficiently good addresses a useful bottleneck in repeated mixed-integer optimization. The reported Gurobi runtime reductions are substantial on five of six families, including MIS (221.0 to 11.7 seconds) and MMCN (245.2 to 83.9 seconds).

Originality: Calibrating a trajectory-level stopping criterion is a meaningful application of conformal prediction. The focus on stopping an exact solver distinguishes the contribution from predicting solutions or validating independent heuristics, although the statistical ingredients are largely established.

Evaluation: The experiments cover six problem families and two solvers. Appendix C includes useful comparisons against linear predictors, incumbent-improvement heuristics, and relaxed solver tolerances; the LSTM offers substantial advantages on several families.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and pipeline are accessible. The paper appropriately acknowledges expensive training-data collection, dependence on the target distribution, and limited benefits when finding and certifying good solutions occur close together. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 4.1 is false as stated, undermining the central guarantee. Consider identical trajectories with true gap g(t)=1 and predicted gap 0.5 for t<1, and both zero thereafter, with epsilon<1. Every threshold k<0.5 stops safely at t=1, so the theorem's supremum is kappa=0.5; the specified <= stopping rule then stops at t=0 and fails with probability one. These trajectories satisfy the stated convergence assumptions. The proof incorrectly treats a supremum as an attained safe maximum, and equivalence (2) fails for plateaus and jumps. A corrected score, boundary convention, and proof aligned with the implemented callback rule are essential.

Soundness—The additional theoretical results also need repair. Theorem 5.1 applies a VC bound for each fixed u and then takes a supremum over all u without establishing a simultaneous bound. Monotonicity may support another proof, but the argument supplied does not justify this step. Theorem 5.3's extension of expected suboptimality and runtime bounds requires penalties scaled by Smax and Tmax, respectively, rather than an unqualified additive rho. Its displayed proofs also use equality where only an inequality involving absolute differences is valid.

Evidence—The reported coverage does not convincingly support the headline reliability claim. Appendix B reports 88% success for CP GRB on MVC and 85%, 78.6%, and 80% for CP COPT on GISP, OTS, and MMCN. A single calibration split can under-cover without contradicting a marginal guarantee, but these results require explicit analysis and uncertainty estimates. Appendix D's repeated-calibration experiment still reports mean coverage of 92.7% and 92.8% at c=100 for CFLP and GISP. Moreover, c=5 and c=10 cannot satisfy n/(c+1)>=0.95 under the stated theorem, yet the alternative calibration convention is not explained.

Significance and experimental validity—All comparisons disable presolve, use one thread, and configure Gurobi with MIPFocus=1. These settings are disclosed, but the absence of experiments with standard presolve and practical solver configurations leaves the general usefulness of the speedups uncertain. The strongest main-text comparisons use stopping after one or three feasible solutions, which provides little quality control. Appendix C improves the comparison, but also shows that simpler alternatives can compete: on OTS, a 1% solver tolerance averages 74.2 seconds versus 96.2 seconds for the proposed method, with very low observed suboptimality. Comparisons should match empirical reliability and include predictor overhead and training-cost amortization.

Reproducibility—The promised code link on page 15 is absent. Important implementation details are missing, including learning rate, feature normalization, sequence sampling, stabilization of the singular weight w(t) proportional to 1/y(t) when y(t)=0, and exact threshold handling. Table 1 lists 800 OTS training instances while its caption says only 100 instances are available in total and assigns all 100 to calibration and testing; the training source and independence of the splits therefore need clarification. The manuscript also does not clearly explain how exact reference optima are obtained for trajectories subject to the 600-second limit.

Presentation—Several inconsistencies affect interpretation rather than merely style. Section 4.2 trains an absolute objective-gap predictor while earlier notation describes a relative-gap predictor; this need not invalidate calibration, but the units and implementation must be explicit. Section 6.2 describes Figure 4 as measuring epsilon-optimality, whereas the figure uses 2epsilon. Its claim of achieving 95% success with high probability also conflates marginal coverage with a stronger calibration-conditional guarantee. Overall, the useful idea and promising speedups do not compensate for an invalid central theorem and unresolved reliability and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: Learning when to stop a solver addresses a useful practical problem: feasible solutions can become near-optimal substantially before branch-and-bound certifies them. The reported Gurobi runtime reductions are substantial on five of six families, including approximately 78% on OTS and 95% on MIS.

Originality: Calibrating an entire stopping trajectory is a meaningful application of conformal prediction, distinct from certifying an independently generated heuristic solution. The solver-state features also make the approach relatively straightforward to integrate.

Evaluation: The experiments cover six problem families and two commercial solvers. Appendix C includes useful comparisons with simpler predictors and relaxed solver tolerances, showing that the learned predictor offers advantages on several families.

Presentation and limitations: The motivation and pipeline are accessible. The paper appropriately acknowledges offline data-generation costs, distributional assumptions, and variation in speedups. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantee: Theorem 4.1 is false as stated because the supremum of safe thresholds need not itself be safe under the stopping rule using ≤. For example, let every instance have true gap 1 before time 1 and 0 afterward, and predicted gap 0.5 before time 1 and 0 afterward, with ε < 1. Every threshold below 0.5 stops safely, so the theorem selects κ = 0.5; that threshold stops immediately and fails on every instance. These trajectories satisfy the convergence assumptions. Equation (2) likewise fails on plateaus. The calibration rule needs explicit treatment of strict inequalities, ties, and discontinuous callback trajectories, followed by a corrected proof.

Soundness—additional theory: Theorem 5.1 applies a VC bound for each fixed u and then takes a supremum over u without establishing a simultaneous probability statement. Theorem 5.3 also claims an additive ρ correction for Theorem 5.1, whereas expectations of variables bounded by Smax or Tmax generally require corrections scaled by those bounds. These issues weaken the claimed stronger guarantees beyond the central theorem.

Coverage evidence: Several reported success rates are substantially below the nominal 95% target: CP COPT achieves 85% on GISP, 78.6% on OTS, and 80% on MMCN; CP GRB achieves 88% on MVC. A single calibration split can underperform a marginal guarantee, so these observations alone do not refute valid conformal coverage, but they require repeated-split evaluation and uncertainty estimates. Table 16 also uses c = 5 and 10, for which no n ≤ c can satisfy n/(c+1) ≥ 0.95; the fallback or changed coverage target is unspecified. Section 6.2 further describes Figure 4 as measuring ε-optimality, although its caption specifies 2ε.

Reproducibility: Table 1 lists 800 OTS training instances while stating that only 100 instances are available in total; the training source and independence of the splits need clarification. Equation (5) specifies weights proportional to 1/y even though y becomes zero when the optimum is found, without explaining regularization. Learning rate, sampling interval, sequence handling, and exact calibration implementation are also missing, and the promised code link is absent.

Practical significance of the evaluation: Presolve is disabled for both solvers without a supporting ablation. Consequently, the large speedups establish benefits under this restricted configuration, but not against normal solver operation. Results with presolve enabled, explicit inference-overhead accounting, and an estimate of how many deployment solves amortize training-data generation would better establish practical value.

Presentation and mathematical consistency: The predictor is introduced as estimating a relative gap but trained against the absolute gap U − z*, leaving its scaling unclear. Section 3.3 also claims that (U − z*)/|z*| ≤ (U − L)/|L| follows from L ≤ z*, which is not generally true for negative objective values. These conventions need correction, particularly because the manuscript treats general mixed-integer objectives.
